headline: Rates Slip Further as Tech Selloff Outweighs Inflation
tileReason: The daily 30-year average dipped to 7.32% Tuesday, a two-week low, and bonds are rallying again this morning as tech stocks slide, even though core inflation came in a bit hot.
takeaway:
Rates eased to a two-week low on Tuesday. Mortgage News Daily's 30-year average slipped to 7.32% from 7.34% Monday, down 0.16% from a week earlier. Other surveys run lower: the Mortgage Research Center showed about 7.13% and Optimal Blue, which tracks rates on loans borrowers actually locked, 7.17% as of Monday.

Falling tech stocks pushed money into bonds. Tech shares gave back much of Monday's surge on Tuesday, with Nvidia down nearly 6%, and the selloff is deepening this morning in the U.S. and overseas. When investors get nervous they tend to buy Treasuries for safety, which pushes yields down. The 10-year Treasury yield, which mortgage rates tend to follow, closed Tuesday near 4.91% and is near 4.84% this morning, down about 0.07% to 0.09%.

This morning's inflation report was a little warm, but bonds shrugged it off. The Fed's preferred inflation measure, the PCE price index, rose 0.3% in October and 3.8% from a year earlier, as expected. The core version, which leaves out food and energy, rose 3.3% from a year earlier, a bit above the 3.2% forecast and up from 3.1%. Normally that would push rates up, but the stock selloff mattered more, and mortgage bond prices are up about a third of a point this morning, which helps lenders offer lower rates.

The economy still looks sturdy. Early reports show third-quarter growth revised up to about 4.3% and new jobless claims falling to about 189,000, both signs of strength that usually work against lower rates. The Mortgage Bankers Association's weekly survey showed its 30-year rate up to 7.38% from 7.35% in the week ending Nov 20, yet purchase applications jumped about 10%.

A December Fed hike is still seen as almost certain. Futures markets (where traders bet on the Fed's next move) put the odds of a quarter-point increase on Dec 9 at about 98% early this morning, with about 2% on no change. These are market expectations, not a Fed forecast.

Lenders still have a cushion. The Optimal Blue conforming index sat about 2.19% above the 10-year Treasury on Nov 17, the latest day recorded, compared with a long-run average of about 1.76%. That extra room gives lenders space to pass along bond rallies like today's.

Bond markets close Thursday for Thanksgiving and close early Friday at 2 PM ET. Freddie Mac's weekly survey comes out today at noon ET instead of Thursday. After the holiday the big tests are the Dec 4 jobs report, the Dec 9 Fed decision and November consumer prices on Dec 10.

fedOdds.note: These are the odds of a quarter-point hike. Readings this morning range from about 98% to nearly 100%. Sources differ on the remainder: this morning's readings put it on no change, while Tuesday evening's put it on a bigger half-point hike.

drivers.title: Tech selloff sends money into bonds
drivers.text: Tech stocks reversed lower Tuesday, with Nvidia down nearly 6%, and the slide is spreading this morning in the U.S. and Asia. Nervous investors buy Treasuries for safety, which lowers yields; the 10-year is down to about 4.84% this morning and mortgage bond prices are up.

drivers.title: Core inflation runs a bit hot
drivers.text: October's core PCE inflation, the Fed's preferred gauge, rose 3.3% from a year earlier, above the 3.2% expected. Hotter inflation usually pushes yields up because it keeps the Fed raising rates, but today it was overshadowed by the stock selloff.

drivers.title: December Fed hike nearly locked in
drivers.text: Futures odds of a quarter-point Fed hike on Dec 9 are about 98% or higher. When investors expect the Fed to keep raising its short-term rate, longer-term yields and mortgage rates have a hard time falling far.

drivers.title: Economy still looks strong
drivers.text: Consumer confidence jumped to 103.3 Tuesday, and early reports this morning show third-quarter growth revised up to about 4.3% and jobless claims near 189,000. A strong economy can keep inflation sticky, which tends to hold rates up.

drivers.title: Mortgage rates still far above Treasuries
drivers.text: The Optimal Blue conforming index sat about 2.19% above the 10-year Treasury yield on Nov 17, compared with a long-run average of about 1.76%. That wide gap gives lenders room to pass along bond rallies.

outlook.baseSource: Mortgage News Daily, Nov 24 close (latest available)
outlook.basis: The odds are close to even. Rates are at a two-week low and bonds are rallying this morning as tech stocks slide, and the gap between mortgage rates and Treasuries is still wide (about 2.19% vs. a long-run average near 1.76%), which leaves room for lenders to cut. Working against borrowers: core inflation came in a bit hot, the economy still looks strong, and a December Fed hike is all but priced in. Big swing events: the Dec 4 jobs report, the Dec 9 Fed decision and its projections, Dec 10 consumer prices, the stock market and oil headlines.
outlook.caveat: This is professional judgment from 30+ years watching these markets, not a guarantee. One oil headline or data surprise can move rates a quarter point in a day.

calendar.label: Wed, Nov 18
calendar.event: October housing starts; MBA weekly mortgage survey; $16B 20-year bond sale (10 AM PT); minutes of the October Fed meeting (11 AM PT)
calendar.why: The minutes show how many officials lean toward more hikes after December, and strong home building signals a sturdy economy.
calendar.actual: Housing starts 1.31M pace, up 9.9% (single-family permits fell 8.7%); MBA 30-year rate 7.35%, up from 7.21%; applications -2.3%; 20-year bond sold at 5.459%, in line with expectations; Fed minutes showed almost all officials expect more hikes
calendar.reaction: The 10-year yield ended about 0.03% lower near 5.07%, helped more by falling oil than by the minutes, and mortgage bond prices rose slightly.

calendar.label: Thu, Nov 19
calendar.event: Weekly jobless claims, Philadelphia Fed factory survey, Freddie Mac weekly rate survey (9 AM PT); Fed speakers Hammack, Jefferson, Goolsbee, Barr and Barkin
calendar.why: Low layoffs keep the job market looking sturdy, which tends to keep rates firm.
calendar.actual: Claims 203K (continuing claims 1.76M, up 70K); Philadelphia Fed factory index 6.3, down from 20.9, with prices paid rising; Freddie Mac 30-year 7.28%, up from 7.11%
calendar.reaction: The 10-year yield ended near 5.05%, down slightly, after stocks fell about 2%, and mortgage bond prices rose.

calendar.label: Fri, Nov 20
calendar.event: Final November consumer sentiment (University of Michigan); Fed Governors Waller (8:25 AM ET) and Cook (12:15 PM ET) speak
calendar.why: Consumers' inflation expectations feed into the Fed's thinking, and Fed comments about more hikes can push rates up.
calendar.actual: 51.5; consumers expect 3.7% inflation over the next year, down from 4.3% early this month, and 3.3% over five years
calendar.surpriseLabel: in line, with lower inflation expectations
calendar.reaction: Stocks fell 3.7% and the 10-year yield dropped about 0.12% to near 4.92%, and lenders cut mortgage rates during the day.

calendar.label: Mon, Nov 23
calendar.event: November business surveys (S&P Global flash PMIs); $69B 2-year note sale; New York Fed President Williams speaks
calendar.why: Williams is one of the Fed's most influential voices, so any hint about the pace of hikes can move rates.
calendar.actual: Williams said inflation near 3.5% is too high and he wouldn't rule out back-to-back hikes; 2-year notes sold at about 4.70%; Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO and the S&P 500 jumped 4.7%
calendar.reaction: The 10-year yield jumped early on the stock rally, then settled about unchanged near 4.92% as oil fell; mortgage rates edged up 0.01%.

calendar.label: Tue, Nov 24
calendar.event: Consumer confidence (Conference Board) and September home prices; $70B 5-year note sale (10 AM PT)
calendar.why: Strong confidence points to a sturdy economy and spending, which tends to push rates up.
calendar.actual: 103.3, highest since January 2025; Case-Shiller 20-city home prices +2.6% from a year earlier (2.7% expected); 5-year notes sold at 4.719%
calendar.reaction: Bonds held up as tech stocks fell; the 10-year ended near 4.91% and the 30-year mortgage average slipped 0.02% to 7.32%.

calendar.label: Wed, Nov 25
calendar.event: October PCE inflation (the Fed's preferred measure), income and spending, Q3 growth revision, durable goods orders and jobless claims (8:30 AM ET); MBA weekly survey; new home sales (10 AM ET); $44B 7-year note sale; Freddie Mac weekly survey (noon ET); Fed Beige Book (2 PM ET)
calendar.why: Hotter inflation would add to the case for more Fed hikes and push rates up.
calendar.actual: 0.3% monthly (3.8% yearly); core 0.3% (3.3% yearly); income +0.7%, inflation-adjusted spending flat; MBA 30-year 7.38%, purchase applications +10%. Early reports (one source so far): Q3 growth revised to 4.3%, jobless claims 189K
calendar.reaction: Yields fell anyway as tech stocks slid; the 2-year dropped to about 4.61% and the 10-year to about 4.84%, and mortgage bond prices rose about 0.33.

talkingPoints.buyers: Mortgage rates eased to a two-week low Tuesday, with the daily 30-year average at 7.32%, and bonds are improving again this morning as tech stocks slide. A December Fed hike still looks nearly certain and inflation is sticky, so the picture can change quickly after the holiday. If you're under contract or close to it, talk with Stuart about how locking, a float-down option (which lets you take a lower rate if rates drop after you lock), or waiting would each fit your closing date.
talkingPoints.sellers: Rates are at their lowest in two weeks, around 7.32%, and purchase mortgage applications jumped about 10% last week. Realistic pricing, or a seller credit buyers can use to lower their rate, can help a home stand out over the holidays.
talkingPoints.oneLiner: Mortgage rates slipped to a two-week low near 7.32% heading into Thanksgiving as a tech stock slide pulled investors into bonds.
